summary:
Armenia decriminalised consensual same-sex conduct in 2003 and has no statute of the restrictive type applied in neighbouring Azerbaijan. Same-sex marriage is prohibited. In 2013 police proposed a bill criminalising 'non-traditional sexual relationships' and LGBT 'propaganda' to young people, modelled on legislation in another country; it failed to pass after a national LGBT organisation argued it served as a distraction tactic.

Legal gender recognition operates as an administrative practice, but the legal change of gender has required surgery since 2006. There is no legal recognition of non-binary gender, and gender-affirming care is restricted.

The framework offers little affirmative protection. There is no discrimination protection on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and the anti-discrimination bill tabled in 2018 did not pass. Hate-crime protection covering bias-motivated violence is characterised as ambiguous since 2022.

The Pink Human Rights Defender NGO's annual report for 2024 documents discrimination, torture and inhuman or degrading treatment including sexual violence, domestic violence and extortion targeting LGBT people, violations of private and family life, and infringements of education and work rights, alongside hate speech. The report carries a chapter on pressure directed at a transgender individual who participated in a beauty pageant.

Trans-specific hostility has been expressed at the highest level of politics. Lilit Martirosyan, Armenia's first registered trans woman and in April 2019 the first transgender person to address the National Assembly, received death threats by Facebook and email after her speech on LGBTI discrimination, with members of parliament calling for her to be burned alive. In February 2020 a member of a nationalist party burned incense over the same lectern to 'cleanse' it, denouncing her speech as a desecration.

Violence against LGBT venues and spaces has drawn a weak official response. In May 2012 a neo-Nazi arson attack on the gay-friendly DIY bar in Yerevan used a Molotov cocktail; police took 12 hours to respond, and two suspects were later identified from CCTV. In November 2018 a Christian LGBT group was forced to cancel planned forums and events after what it described as constant threats and organised intimidation from political and religious leaders, and it reported that police were not ready to protect them.

Public expression carries a measurable cost. In 2017 organisers of the Yerevan International Film Festival cancelled the screening of two LGBT-themed films after negative public reaction. In 2014 the Iravunk newspaper published a list of dozens of Armenian LGBT Facebook accounts and called them 'zombies'; the Court of Appeals ruled that the newspaper had not offended anyone and ordered the plaintiffs to pay 50,000 dram (about US$120) to the newspaper. Public-acceptance scores for LGBT people are very low, at 5 out of 100, and a 2012 study found that 55% of Armenians would end a relationship with a friend or relative who came out while 70% regard LGBT people as 'strange'.
tangentialFactors:
Armenia sits between jurisdictions moving in opposite directions: Azerbaijan retains criminal penalties for consensual same-sex conduct, while Georgia is the third point of comparison in regional assessments. Armenia's own 2013 bill was expressly modelled on legislation adopted in another country, and it failed rather than being struck down.

The ILGA-Europe and COC fact-finding report 'Forced Out: LGBT People in Armenia' (February 2009) is the standing historical baseline for the country's conditions, covering visibility and coming out, societal and institutional homophobia, media coverage, harassment, violence, discrimination and the legislation then in force. It predates both the 2003 analysis of repeal and the 2024 documentation, so conditions it describes should be read as the earlier state of the same pattern.

Social attitudes rather than formal law are the more reliable predictor of friction on the ground: acceptance scores of 5/100, the 2012 finding that 55% would end a relationship with someone who came out, and 70% who find LGBT people 'strange'. The 2017 film-festival cancellations and the 2014 newspaper list show private actors restricting LGBT visibility where no law does.
localsOnly:
The Pink Human Rights Defender NGO (Pink Armenia) is the principal domestic documentation body: its annual report on the human rights situation of LGBT+ people in Armenia for 2024 catalogues discrimination, torture and inhuman or degrading treatment including sexual violence, domestic violence and extortion, violations of private and family life, education and work rights, and hate speech, and it is the source that tracks pressure on an individual trans person around a beauty pageant.

Residents seeking legal gender change must meet the surgical requirement in force since 2006, and no non-binary status exists in the civil-registry framework. Gender-affirming care is restricted for residents as well as visitors.

Domestic advocacy history includes the defeat of the 2013 criminalisation proposal after Pink Armenia argued it was a distraction tactic, the failure of the anti-discrimination bill tabled in 2018, and the November 2018 cancellation of a Christian LGBT group's forums under threats from political and religious leaders. Litigation has gone against LGBT plaintiffs: the Court of Appeals held that the Iravunk newspaper's publication of a list of LGBT Facebook accounts caused no offence and ordered the plaintiffs to pay 50,000 dram to the newspaper.
outOfScopeNotes:
The scope of the 'ambiguous' hate-crime characterisation after 2022 is unresolved in the sources: no provision, penalty range or case outcome is supplied, and enforcement practice is not sourced.

The sources do not state whether the surgical requirement for legal gender change applies to foreign visitors, whether Armenia's authorities recognise gender markers changed abroad, or what documents are examined at entry. No information is available here on visa screening, border questioning, or the treatment of mismatched passport markers.

The precise statutory article repealed in 2003 and the terms of the 2013 police proposal are not reproduced in the inventory; only its failure to pass and the organisation's characterisation of it are documented.

Restrictions on gender-affirming care are stated without detail as to which treatments are limited and by which authority. The 2024 report's allegations of torture and sexual violence are documented by a non-governmental organisation and no corresponding prosecutions or official findings are sourced.

The ILGA-Europe/COC report dates from February 2009 and its findings on conditions, media coverage and legislation describe that period; no source in the inventory confirms which of those findings still hold.
